findings.title: Reciprocal carrying: bodily care and entrusted acknowledgment
findings.claim: A reversal of burdens: maternal carrying generates, but does not mechanically purchase, the child's entrusted practice of recognition.
findings.mechanism: The divine enjoining is connected to the parent-child relation. The mother first carries the human inwardly; the later imperative places recognition of that favor on the once-carried addressee. These local clauses reverse the direction of carrying without equating bodily pregnancy and ethical acknowledgment.
findings.reader_payoff: The child first appears as the one carried and later as the addressee charged to acknowledge received care.
findings.containment: The link between bodily carrying and ethical response is an attributed analogy, not a claim that the verb lexically means gratitude or that care mechanically earns repayment. The two burdens remain distinct.

findings.title: Origin and destination: embodied source and final return
findings.claim: The verse coordinates unequal directions: parents disclose embodied origin and care, while God alone names the final becoming and homeward endpoint.

findings.reader_payoff: The mother and the paired parents mark an embodied human source; the closing phrase directs final return toward God.
findings.containment: The home/settlement branch is a metaphorical endpoint, not a claim that God is a physical location. Human parents and God are coordinated as gratitude recipients but are not made equal sources or endpoints.
